fetched_contents.text: Dynamic Assessment in L2 Settings: A Systematic Review and a Meta-Analysis[v1] This version is not peer-reviewed. Abstract Dynamic assessment (DA) is an approach that intentionally brings instruction and learning together through adopting a social-constructivist framework in order to assess, diagnose, and improve L2 linguistic skills. DA in the L2 classroom has been applied but not surveyed for its effect and plausibility. To address that, I did a systematic review and a meta-analysis to report the effectiveness of DA in the L2 classroom in developing students’ linguistic skills. Nine databases were searched to ensure a comprehensive coverage of the field including published dissertations. The characteristics of the studies were coded and analyzed systematically following a developed coding sheet. Means and standard deviations were coded, and the standardized mean difference was used to calculate effect sizes. A random effects model was used to compute the overall effect size of the included studies in the meta-analysis. Results indicated a positive effect of DA on the development of foreign language skills. The magnitude of the effect was significantly large (g = 1.07; 95% CI = [0.82, 1.32]). The prediction intervals suggested that future research that meets inclusion criteria will report 95% of the time a positive effect (95% PI = [0.03, 2.10]). Sample size, age, and targeted linguistic skill did not significantly change the existing effect of DA in the L2 classroom. Based on the systematic review and existing literature, a framework was developed to help pedagogists include DA in their L2 classroom practices by explicating its purposes and functions, and the required conditions for a successful implementation. Keywords: Dynamic Assessment ; Second/Foreign Language Learning ; Assessment ; Sociocultural Theory ; Vygotsky Dynamic Assessment in L2 Settings: A Systematic Review and a Meta-Analysis Assessment in the classroom context is a delicate exploration of growing minds influenced by interpersonal and intrapersonal factors with a set of priori assumptions regarding the subject-matter’s nature and process of its acquisition. McMillan (2013, p.4) described classroom assessment as: “… a process that teachers and students use in collecting, evaluating, and using evidence of student learning for a variety of purposes, including diagnosing student strengths and weaknesses, monitoring student progress toward meeting desired levels of proficiency, assigning grades, and providing feedback to parents.” Shepard (2000) described the role of assessment in teaching and learning and predicted that an elaboration of a social-constructivist framework will be “… the middle-ground theory that will be accepted as common wisdom and carried into practice” (p. 6). She suggested that dynamic assessment is a very helpful “interactive assessment” that could move assessment into the ongoing teaching instead of being an “end-point of instruction” (p. 10). One of the most celebrated types of assessment in the classroom is formative assessment. Yet, formative assessment is not clearly defined (Bennet, 2011), which needs to “… transform from a collection of abstract theories and research methodologies and become a creative and systematic classroom practice” (Clark, 2012, p. 24). On the other hand, a less widely implemented type of assessment, dynamic assessment, draws from the work of the psychologist Lev Vygotsky and his well-known zone of proximal development (ZPD) (Elliot, 2003). Dynamic assessment (DA) is an intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together (van der Veen, Dobber, & van Oers, 2016) which aims to modify the cognitive situation through teaching (Tzuriel, 2001). Elliot (2003) encouraged the production of DA research that produces applicable practices for teachers, amongst others, but it seems that such call is not answered (Elliot, Resing, & Bechmann, 2018). In the world of second/foreign language teaching, the scene seems to be a bit different. Kozulin and Garb’s (2002) study was among the first to apply dynamic assessment (DA) in second language (L2) learning, influencing future research. Using a pretest-intervention-posttest design, they aimed to improve English text comprehension by mediating cognitive strategies (Feuerstein, 1979; 1990). The study involved 23 low-performing EFL students. After mediation, students showed significant improvement with an effect size of 1.2. They also developed a learning potential score (LPS) formula, now widely used to classify students based on future learning potential. Mediation was sandwiched between tests, illustrating DA’s feasibility in L2 classrooms. Sternberg and Grigorenko (2002, pp. 28-29) distinguished between static and dynamic testing. Importantly, dynamic testing explores “whether and how the participant will change if an opportunity is provided”, while dynamic assessment is an intentional attempt to “intervene and change” (Sternberg & Grigorenko, 2002, p. 30). Poehner (2008) argues that such distinction is unnecessary as change can occur even in a single session of mediation (p. 18). Another distinction adopted by many of the reviewed L2 DA papers is Lantolf and Poehner’s (2004) distinction of two types of mediation: interventionist and interactionist. Interventionist DA follows a standardized format in which mediation is predetermined to help the learner(s) reach a predetermined reach point; on the other hand, interactionist DA offers mediation as it emerges between the learner(s) and the mediator in which an end point is not of any concern, nor the effort and time needed for development (p. 54). The less frequent use of dynamic assessment in educational settings could be due to different reasons. Dynamic assessment is a formative assessment approach that merges assessment and instruction, with the purpose of identifying learners’ potential development rather than merely measuring their current ability. Its core principles are rooted in sociocultural theory and the zone of proximal development, where assessment is not static but interactive and mediated. In the evidence provided, dynamic assessment is described as “a formative type of assessment that combines the assessment process with the learning process” [N1-R3], and as “an intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together” [N3-F2]. The purpose is therefore to assess students’ potential development as a predictor of future individual performance, not only what they can do now [N2-F1].

Dynamic assessment differs from static or summative testing in several ways. Static or summative testing typically evaluates current performance in isolation and is often used for grading or certification [N3-R5]. In contrast, dynamic assessment is interactive, responsive, and diagnostic. It is designed to measure not only a learner’s current language proficiency but mainly their learning potential [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that dynamic assessment explores “whether and how the participant will change if an opportunity is provided,” whereas static testing is more about current ability [N3-F2]. This distinction is important because dynamic assessment is meant to be a “middle-ground theory” that moves assessment into ongoing teaching rather than treating it as an end-point of instruction [N3-F2].

A key feature of dynamic assessment is the role of scaffolding and instructional intervention. The evidence shows that mediation—helping learners through scaffolding—is central to dynamic assessment. In the Spanish classroom study, students were allowed to use different sorts of mediation in order to complete their assigned task [N2-F1]. The same study also states that mediation was only effective when the concepts were in the students’ zone of proximal development, indicating that scaffolding is not arbitrary but targeted to learners’ developmental readiness [N2-F1]. Another source explicitly says that dynamic assessment “insists on the inseparability of assessment and instruction,” focusing on learners’ potential development rather than their present problem-solving abilities [N1-R1]. This means that dynamic assessment is not simply an evaluation tool; it is an instructional intervention that is embedded within the assessment process [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Overall, dynamic assessment in L2 education is best understood as a dynamic, interactive, and intervention-oriented assessment method that seeks to diagnose learning potential and support development through scaffolding and mediation [N1-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2].

Dynamic assessment is applied in L2 Spanish education primarily in classroom settings where the goal is to diagnose learning potential, inform instruction, and support oral or linguistic development. The evidence points to a university-level beginner Spanish classroom, where 30 students were assessed in pairs using a picture-based task to evaluate oral ability in giving and receiving directions in Spanish [N2-F1]. In that study, the classroom setting was not a traditional testing environment but an instructional one: students were allowed to use different sorts of mediation in order to complete their assigned task [N2-F1]. This suggests that dynamic assessment is most commonly used in formative or diagnostic classroom settings rather than in high-stakes standardized testing environments.

Examples of tasks, materials, and formats used in practice include picture-based oral performance tasks, interviews, and mediation-supported activities. The Spanish classroom study used three specially designed photos to evaluate oral ability and an interview format [N2-F1]. The same source describes the task as a cognitive developmental activity to assess oral proficiency in a beginner Spanish course [N2-F1]. Another example comes from a broader Spanish classroom study, which notes that dynamic assessment can be used in oral tests and that the results can foster students’ development in the process of second language acquisition [N2-F1]. In addition, the evidence includes a classroom teacher’s efforts to implement DA principles in daily Spanish instruction, indicating that dynamic assessment is also used in everyday classroom activities rather than only in isolated assessments [N2-R3].

Teachers interpret and use the results of dynamic assessment as a guide for instruction and intervention. In the Spanish classroom study, the researchers concluded that assessment has to be a dynamic process to conceptualize a valid prognosis of the learner’s potential development [N2-F1]. The study also suggests that DA procedures can act as a mediational tool in oral tests to foster development [N2-F1]. Another source states that DA can serve various functions in L2 contexts, including diagnosing student weaknesses, informing instruction, and acting as a placement or diagnostic tool [N3-R4]. This means teachers do not treat dynamic assessment as a final score but as a way to understand where a student is likely to develop and what support they may need next.

The evidence also notes limitations and contextual constraints that shape how dynamic assessment is used in practice. One source highlights that many dynamic assessments are devised by psychologists and can be difficult to apply in educational settings [N3-F2]. Another source notes that standardized test scores must be compared with results from informal measures, especially in linguistically diverse contexts [N4-R5]. These points imply that dynamic assessment is often used alongside other methods and is not universally easy to implement. Nonetheless, the evidence indicates that in Spanish classrooms, it is used mainly in oral, interview-based, and task-based formats, with teachers interpreting the results as a basis for scaffolding and instructional planning [N2-F1][N2-R3][N3-R4].

First, dynamic assessment is presented as a way to measure learning potential rather than just current proficiency. One source states that dynamic assessments are designed to measure not only a learner’s current language proficiency but mainly their learning potential [N3-R5]. Another source says DA is an intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together, aiming to modify the cognitive situation through teaching [N3-F2]. This makes dynamic assessment especially useful for identifying students’ capacity to develop, not only their current level of performance.

Second, the evidence supports improved instruction and intervention planning. A systematic review and meta-analysis reports that DA has a significantly large positive effect on the development of foreign language skills, with a standardized mean difference of g = 1.07 [N3-F2]. This indicates that DA is not just an assessment tool but an instructional intervention that can improve learning outcomes. The same review also notes that DA can serve various functions in L2 contexts, including diagnosing student weaknesses and informing instruction [N3-R4]. In the Spanish classroom study, DA procedures were used as a mediational tool in oral tests, and the study concluded that the dynamic process helps conceptualize a valid prognosis of the learner’s potential development [N2-F1]. These findings support the idea that dynamic assessment provides more useful information for teachers to plan targeted instruction and support.

Third, the evidence points to better student outcomes and engagement. The systematic review and meta-analysis found a positive effect of DA on the development of foreign language skills, with a large effect size [N3-F2]. The same source also notes that sample size, age, and targeted linguistic skill did not significantly change the existing effect of DA in the L2 classroom [N3-F2]. This suggests that dynamic assessment can have broad and consistent positive effects across different contexts. In the Spanish classroom study, the use of DA was associated with students’ development in the process of second language acquisition [N2-F1]. Another source describes DA as a helpful “interactive assessment” that can move assessment into the ongoing teaching process rather than treating it as an end-point of instruction [N3-F2]. This aligns with the idea that dynamic assessment supports more engaged, ongoing learning rather than passive testing.

The evidence also indirectly supports the advantages of dynamic assessment over traditional methods by showing that traditional assessments are often less suitable for bilingual or linguistically diverse learners. For example, one study examines dynamic assessment’s added value over traditional assessments for identifying Spanish-speaking English learners’ risk for developing certain outcomes [N5-R1]. Another source notes that few standardized tests are available in languages other than Spanish and that standardized test scores must be compared with results from informal measures [N4-R5]. This implies that traditional tests may be less informative or less applicable in some L2 Spanish contexts, while dynamic assessment can provide richer diagnostic information [N4-R5][N5-R1].

Overall, the evidence suggests that dynamic assessment is advantageous because it identifies learning potential, improves instruction and intervention planning, and can lead to better student outcomes and engagement [N3-R5][N3-F2][N3-R4][N2-F1]. However, the evidence also indicates that these advantages are best realized when dynamic assessment is used interactively and as part of a broader assessment framework, rather than as a replacement for traditional methods alone [N3-F2][N4-R5].

## How dynamic assessment is utilized in second language (L2) Spanish education

In the evidence provided, dynamic assessment is described as “a formative type of assessment that combines the assessment process with the learning process” [N1-R3], and as an “intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together” [N3-F2]. This means it is not a passive evaluation tool, but an interactive process that is embedded in the classroom and responsive to learners’ needs [N2-F1].

In L2 Spanish education, dynamic assessment is most commonly applied in **classroom settings** where the goal is to **diagnose learning potential**, **inform instruction**, and **support oral or linguistic development** [N8]. The evidence points to specific classroom examples such as a university-level beginner Spanish classroom, where 30 students were assessed in pairs using a **picture-based oral task** to evaluate oral ability in giving and receiving directions in Spanish [N2-F1]. A teacher’s implementation of DA principles in daily Spanish instruction also shows that dynamic assessment is used in everyday classroom activities, not only in isolated assessments [N2-R3].

## How dynamic assessment differs from traditional assessment

Dynamic assessment differs from traditional assessment in three key ways: **it is interactive rather than static**, **it focuses on learning potential rather than current ability**, and **it integrates scaffolding and instructional intervention** [N7].

First, dynamic assessment is **interactive and diagnostic**, whereas traditional testing is often **static or summative**. Traditional assessments typically evaluate current performance in isolation and are often used for grading or certification [N3-R5]. In contrast, dynamic assessment explores “whether and how the participant will change if an opportunity is provided,” and is described as an “interactive assessment” that moves assessment into the ongoing teaching process rather than treating it as an end-point of instruction [N3-F2]. This makes dynamic assessment especially useful for identifying learning potential and for guiding future instruction [N3-R5][N3-F2].

Second, dynamic assessment is designed to measure **learning potential** rather than just current proficiency. One source states that dynamic assessments are designed to measure not only a learner’s current language proficiency but mainly their learning potential [N3-R5]. Another source says DA is an intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together, aiming to modify the cognitive situation through teaching [N3-F2]. This means dynamic assessment is better suited to diagnosing weaknesses and predicting future development than many traditional tests [N3-R4][N2-F1].

In the Spanish classroom study, students were allowed to use different sorts of mediation to complete their assigned task [N2-F1]. The same study also states that mediation was only effective when the concepts were in the students’ **zone of proximal development** [N2-F1]. This shows that scaffolding is not arbitrary: it is targeted to learners’ developmental readiness and is part of the assessment process itself [N1-R1][N3-F2]. In other words, dynamic assessment is not just an evaluation; it is an instructional intervention embedded within the assessment [N2-F1][N3-F2].

In practice, dynamic assessment in L2 Spanish education is used in **specific classroom or instructional settings** where teachers want to support development rather than simply judge performance. ## Comparison with other assessment types in Spanish classrooms

In Spanish language education, common assessment types include **traditional tests**, **interviews**, **observational methods**, and **informal measures**. The evidence indicates that traditional standardized measures are sometimes used, but they are often supplemented or compared with informal measures because **few standardized tests are available in languages other than Spanish** [N4-R5]. One source also mentions **daily interviews and surveys among students** as ways to collect proficiency-level data [N5-R4]. These examples show that Spanish classrooms frequently use a **mixture of formal and informal assessment methods** [N5-R4][N4-R5].

Dynamic assessment compares with traditional tests, interviews, and observational methods by being more **interactive, diagnostic, and intervention-oriented**. Traditional tests typically evaluate current proficiency and are often summative [N3-R5]. Interviews and observational methods are more informal and qualitative but can still be limited in their ability to predict future learning potential [N5-R4]. In contrast, dynamic assessment is explicitly designed to measure **not only current ability but mainly learning potential** [N3-R5]. It is described as an “interactive assessment” that moves assessment into the ongoing teaching process rather than treating it as an end-point of instruction [N3-F2]. ## Limitations and practical considerations

Although dynamic assessment offers clear advantages, the evidence also indicates some **limitations and challenges**. One source notes that many dynamic assessments are devised by psychologists and can be difficult to apply in educational settings [N3-F2]. Another source highlights that **standardized test scores must always be compared with results from informal measures**, especially in linguistically diverse contexts [N4-R5]. These points imply that dynamic assessment is often used alongside other methods and is not universally easy to implement [N3-F2][N4-R5]. Nonetheless, the evidence suggests that in Spanish education, dynamic assessment is best used as a **complementary rather than standalone** approach, particularly when teachers want to support placement, diagnosis, and formative instruction [N3-R4][N4-R5].

## Conclusion

Overall, dynamic assessment is a powerful tool in L2 Spanish education because it is **interactive, diagnostic, and intervention-oriented**. It differs from traditional assessment by focusing on **learning potential rather than current ability**, embedding **scaffolding and instruction** within assessment, and supporting **formative use** in classroom settings [N7]. In practice, it is used in **oral proficiency assessments**, **interview formats**, and **task-based formats** to inform instruction and support development [N8]. The evidence supports several advantages over traditional methods: better identification of learning potential, improved instruction or intervention planning, and better student outcomes or engagement [N9]. At the same time, it is best understood as one part of a broader assessment framework rather than a replacement for traditional tests, interviews, or observational methods [N10][N3-F2]. Dynamic assessment is a formative assessment approach that merges assessment and instruction, with the purpose of identifying learners’ potential development rather than merely measuring their current ability. Its core principles are rooted in sociocultural theory and the zone of proximal development, where assessment is not static but interactive and mediated. In the evidence provided, dynamic assessment is described as “a formative type of assessment that combines the assessment process with the learning process” [N1-R3], and as “an intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together” [N3-F2]. The purpose is therefore to assess students’ potential development as a predictor of future individual performance, not only what they can do now [N2-F1].

Dynamic assessment differs from static or summative testing in several ways. Static or summative testing typically evaluates current performance in isolation and is often used for grading or certification [N3-R5]. In contrast, dynamic assessment is interactive, responsive, and diagnostic. It is designed to measure not only a learner’s current language proficiency but mainly their learning potential [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that dynamic assessment explores “whether and how the participant will change if an opportunity is provided,” whereas static testing is more about current ability [N3-F2]. This distinction is important because dynamic assessment is meant to be a “middle-ground theory” that moves assessment into ongoing teaching rather than treating it as an end-point of instruction [N3-F2].

A key feature of dynamic assessment is the role of scaffolding and instructional intervention. The evidence shows that mediation—helping learners through scaffolding—is central to dynamic assessment. In the Spanish classroom study, students were allowed to use different sorts of mediation in order to complete their assigned task [N2-F1]. The same study also states that mediation was only effective when the concepts were in the students’ zone of proximal development, indicating that scaffolding is not arbitrary but targeted to learners’ developmental readiness [N2-F1]. Another source explicitly says that dynamic assessment “insists on the inseparability of assessment and instruction,” focusing on learners’ potential development rather than their present problem-solving abilities [N1-R1]. This means that dynamic assessment is not simply an evaluation tool; it is an instructional intervention that is embedded within the assessment process [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Overall, dynamic assessment in L2 education is best understood as a dynamic, interactive, and intervention-oriented assessment method that seeks to diagnose learning potential and support development through scaffolding and mediation [N1-R1][N2-F1][N3-F2].

Dynamic assessment is applied in L2 Spanish education primarily in classroom settings where the goal is to diagnose learning potential, inform instruction, and support oral or linguistic development. The evidence points to a university-level beginner Spanish classroom, where 30 students were assessed in pairs using a picture-based task to evaluate oral ability in giving and receiving directions in Spanish [N2-F1]. In that study, the classroom setting was not a traditional testing environment but an instructional one: students were allowed to use different sorts of mediation in order to complete their assigned task [N2-F1]. This suggests that dynamic assessment is most commonly used in formative or diagnostic classroom settings rather than in high-stakes standardized testing environments.

Examples of tasks, materials, and formats used in practice include picture-based oral performance tasks, interviews, and mediation-supported activities. The Spanish classroom study used three specially designed photos to evaluate oral ability and an interview format [N2-F1]. The same source describes the task as a cognitive developmental activity to assess oral proficiency in a beginner Spanish course [N2-F1]. Another example comes from a broader Spanish classroom study, which notes that dynamic assessment can be used in oral tests and that the results can foster students’ development in the process of second language acquisition [N2-F1]. In addition, the evidence includes a classroom teacher’s efforts to implement DA principles in daily Spanish instruction, indicating that dynamic assessment is also used in everyday classroom activities rather than only in isolated assessments [N2-R3].

Teachers interpret and use the results of dynamic assessment as a guide for instruction and intervention. In the Spanish classroom study, the researchers concluded that assessment has to be a dynamic process to conceptualize a valid prognosis of the learner’s potential development [N2-F1]. The study also suggests that DA procedures can act as a mediational tool in oral tests to foster development [N2-F1]. Another source states that DA can serve various functions in L2 contexts, including diagnosing student weaknesses, informing instruction, and acting as a placement or diagnostic tool [N3-R4]. This means teachers do not treat dynamic assessment as a final score but as a way to understand where a student is likely to develop and what support they may need next.

The evidence also notes limitations and contextual constraints that shape how dynamic assessment is used in practice. One source highlights that many dynamic assessments are devised by psychologists and can be difficult to apply in educational settings [N3-F2]. Another source notes that standardized test scores must be compared with results from informal measures, especially in linguistically diverse contexts [N4-R5]. These points imply that dynamic assessment is often used alongside other methods and is not universally easy to implement. Nonetheless, the evidence indicates that in Spanish classrooms, it is used mainly in oral, interview-based, and task-based formats, with teachers interpreting the results as a basis for scaffolding and instructional planning [N2-F1][N2-R3][N3-R4].

The evidence supports several advantages of dynamic assessment over traditional methods, particularly in identifying learning potential, improving instruction or intervention planning, and showing better student outcomes or engagement. First, dynamic assessment is presented as a way to measure learning potential rather than just current proficiency. One source states that dynamic assessments are designed to measure not only a learner’s current language proficiency but mainly their learning potential [N3-R5]. Another source says DA is an intentional attempt to bring assessment and instruction together, aiming to modify the cognitive situation through teaching [N3-F2]. This makes dynamic assessment especially useful for identifying students’ capacity to develop, not only their current level of performance.

Second, the evidence supports improved instruction and intervention planning. A systematic review and meta-analysis reports that DA has a significantly large positive effect on the development of foreign language skills, with a standardized mean difference of g = 1.07 [N3-F2]. This indicates that DA is not just an assessment tool but an instructional intervention that can improve learning outcomes. The same review also notes that DA can serve various functions in L2 contexts, including diagnosing student weaknesses and informing instruction [N3-R4]. In the Spanish classroom study, DA procedures were used as a mediational tool in oral tests, and the study concluded that the dynamic process helps conceptualize a valid prognosis of the learner’s potential development [N2-F1]. These findings support the idea that dynamic assessment provides more useful information for teachers to plan targeted instruction and support.

Third, the evidence points to better student outcomes and engagement. The systematic review and meta-analysis found a positive effect of DA on the development of foreign language skills, with a large effect size [N3-F2]. The same source also notes that sample size, age, and targeted linguistic skill did not significantly change the existing effect of DA in the L2 classroom [N3-F2]. This suggests that dynamic assessment can have broad and consistent positive effects across different contexts. In the Spanish classroom study, the use of DA was associated with students’ development in the process of second language acquisition [N2-F1]. Another source describes DA as a helpful “interactive assessment” that can move assessment into the ongoing teaching process rather than treating it as an end-point of instruction [N3-F2]. This aligns with the idea that dynamic assessment supports more engaged, ongoing learning rather than passive testing.

The evidence also indirectly supports the advantages of dynamic assessment over traditional methods by showing that traditional assessments are often less suitable for bilingual or linguistically diverse learners. For example, one study examines dynamic assessment’s added value over traditional assessments for identifying Spanish-speaking English learners’ risk for developing certain outcomes [N5-R1]. Another source notes that few standardized tests are available in languages other than Spanish and that standardized test scores must be compared with results from informal measures [N4-R5]. This implies that traditional tests may be less informative or less applicable in some L2 Spanish contexts, while dynamic assessment can provide richer diagnostic information [N4-R5][N5-R1].

Overall, the evidence suggests that dynamic assessment is advantageous because it identifies learning potential, improves instruction and intervention planning, and can lead to better student outcomes and engagement [N3-R5][N3-F2][N3-R4][N2-F1]. However, the evidence also indicates that these advantages are best realized when dynamic assessment is used interactively and as part of a broader assessment framework, rather than as a replacement for traditional methods alone [N3-F2][N4-R5].

Dynamic assessment differs from traditional assessment in three key ways: **it is interactive rather than static**, **it focuses on learning potential rather than current ability**, and **it integrates scaffolding and instructional intervention** [N7].

First, dynamic assessment is **interactive and diagnostic**, whereas traditional testing is often **static or summative**. Traditional assessments typically evaluate current performance in isolation and are often used for grading or certification [N3-R5].
